accordion.title: Accordion
accordion.intro: A vertically stacked set of interactive headings with expandable content.
accordion.singleStateDesc: When a new accordion opens, the other open one closes.
accordion.multiStateDesc: When a new accordion opens, the other open ones don't close.
accordion.richItemsDesc: AccordionItemComplex with flexible slots for avatars, badges, and rich content.
accordion.accessibleA: Yes. It adheres to WAI-ARIA standards and is fully keyboard navigable.
accordion.styledA: Yes. It comes with default styles that integrate seamlessly with your design system.
accordion.animatedA: Yes. It features smooth expand/collapse animations with cubic-bezier easing.
accordion.faq1Content1: An accordion component that organizes content into expandable sections.
accordion.faq1Content2: Click on any trigger to reveal the associated content panel.
accordion.faq2Content1: Use the global theme switcher in the navbar to change the accordion variant.
accordion.faq2Content2: All accordion components will update automatically to match the selected theme.
accordion.faq3Title: Can I use it with multiple sections open?
accordion.faq3Content1: Yes, set the type prop to "multiple" on the Accordion to allow multiple items open simultaneously.
accordion.faq3Content2: For single-expand behavior, use type="single" with the collapsible prop.
accordion.sarahBio: Sarah is a product designer with 5+ years of experience in creating user-centered digital experiences.
accordion.mikeBio: Mike is a full-stack engineer specializing in React, Node.js, and cloud infrastructure.

galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks1TabDescription: A columns-based wall of photography at varying heights, each frame captioned with where it was taken.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks1Intro: Nine frames from recent shoots, arranged into a single wall that lets each image keep its own natural height instead of forcing a uniform crop.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2TabDescription: A uniform thumbnail grid that opens into a full-size lightbox with previous/next controls and a running count.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Heading: Click any frame to see it full size
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Intro: A grid of even thumbnails that opens into a single full-size view — step through the set without ever leaving the lightbox.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo1Caption: A quiet still life shot against soft natural light.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo2Caption: Cactus flowers opening just after sunrise.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo3Caption: Downtown blocks viewed from the fortieth floor.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo4Caption: A macro study of a tidepool at low tide.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo5Caption: A drawer of hand-set wood type, sorted by size.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo6Caption: Fishing boats wrapped in early-morning fog.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo7Caption: Stacked spice cones at an open-air market.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks2Photo8Caption: A commuter train blurred through a long exposure.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks3TabDescription: A photo grid with a category filter bar — narrow the set down to one theme or leave it on All.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks3Intro: Ten frames grouped into four loose themes. Filter down to one, or leave it on All to see the whole set at once.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks4TabDescription: A drag-to-reveal comparison slider for showing an edit, retouch, or staging pass against the original.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks4Heading: Drag to compare before and after
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks4Intro: Three edits, side by side. Drag the handle — or use the arrow keys once it's focused — to reveal how much changed.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks4Example1AfterAlt: Same landscape after a warm color grade
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks4Example2BeforeAlt: Portrait straight out of the camera
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks4Example2AfterAlt: Portrait after skin and light retouching
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks5TabDescription: One large-format frame at a time, edge-to-edge, with arrow controls and a row of jump-to dots.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks5Heading: A full-bleed slideshow of the collection
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks5Intro: Six wide-format frames, shown one at a time. Swipe, use the arrows, or jump straight to a frame with the dots below.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks6TabDescription: Instant-style prints pinned at scattered angles across a corkboard — hover or focus one to bring it forward.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks6Intro: A handful of instant-style prints, each tilted a little differently and pinned in place. Hover or tab to any one to bring it to the front.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks7TabDescription: A scroll-snapping horizontal strip of frames styled like a contact sheet, with arrow controls for stepping through it.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks7Heading: Scroll the strip like a roll of film
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks7Intro: Ten frames laid out edge to edge, snapping into place as you scroll — or use the arrows to step through them one at a time.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks8TabDescription: An asymmetric bento grid of photographs where each tile reveals its title and tag on hover or focus.
galleryBlocks.galleryBlocks8Intro: Nine images arranged into an asymmetric grid, each one a slightly different size. Hover or focus a tile to bring up its title and tag.

about.heading: About Us
about.intro: We are a team of makers, engineers, and storytellers who believe great products come from curiosity, care, and close collaboration.
about.workplaceParagraph1: Our studio is a quiet corner of the internet — a place where small, focused teams ship work that feels personal. Every project starts with a conversation and ends with something we are proud to put our name on.
about.workplaceParagraph2: We keep the team small on purpose. That way every person owns their work end to end, every idea gets heard, and quality never becomes a negotiation.
about.teamBio: Acme Inc. builds tools for teams that move fast. For a decade we have helped product teams turn rough ideas into software people actually enjoy using — from first prototype to worldwide launch.
about.teamPhilosophyParagraph: We believe the best software is opinionated. It makes a few decisions well instead of deferring everything to the user. Every feature we ship has to earn its place by solving a real problem simply.
about.teamValuesParagraph: Clarity over cleverness, feedback over approval, and small autonomous teams over large committees. We hire for judgment and trust people to own their work end to end.
about.teamClosing: We are always looking for curious people to join the team. If our philosophy resonates with you, we would love to hear from you.
about.a1Heading: We exist to make complex things feel simple
about.a1Subtext: Every day we ask the same question: how do we turn an idea into something people actually love? The answer shapes everything we build.
about.a1MissionBody: We build software that respects people's time. That means fewer, sharper features — tools that get out of the way and let teams focus on the work that matters.
about.a1Value1Body: Every feature starts with a real problem a real person has. We listen first, build second, and let usage decide what survives.
about.a1Value2Body: We ship, measure, and iterate. Small experiments every week beat a big bet every year.
about.a1Value3Body: We would rather ship one thing that works beautifully than ten things that work okay.
about.a1Quote: The best products don't ask for more of your attention — they earn it back.
about.tabWithStatsDescription: Photo grid, stats and client logos
about.a2Heading: A small team with a big reach
about.a2Body: We are a remote-first company of builders spread across twelve time zones. Small by design, global by choice.
about.a2Why1: You work directly with the people who build — no account managers in between.
about.a2Why2: Fixed timelines and honest estimates. If something shifts, you hear it from us first.
about.a2Why3: Your code is yours. Clean, documented, and portable from day one.
about.a3Body: We started in a garage with two laptops and a whiteboard. Today we are a distributed team shipping products for companies on every continent — but the garage mentality is still the whole culture.
about.a3Aside: We believe the future of work is small, empowered teams armed with great tools. Our job is to build those tools.
about.a3CardBody: Every project is led end to end by a compact squad — no hand-offs, no committees, just people who care about the outcome.
about.a3SectionText: We pair deep technical expertise with a relentless focus on the user. Weekly demos keep everyone honest, and every release is measured against the goals we agreed on at the start.
about.a3Achievement3Body: where our users work every day
about.a4Body: A good product is a promise. A great product is a promise kept, year after year, by the people who made it.
about.a4Who1Body: Designers who write code and engineers who care about pixels.
about.a4Who2Body: We read, we travel, we break things — and bring what we learn back to work.
about.a4Who3Body: Transparent roadmaps, public retrospectives, honest numbers.
about.a4CtaHeading: We are always hiring curious people
about.a4CtaBody: If you want to own your work end to end, we should talk.
about.a5Caption: Every line of code we ship is code we would want to maintain ourselves.
about.a5StoryBody: We got tired of tooling that talks about developer experience without practicing it. So we built our own: boring-by-default, predictable, and fast enough that you forget it is there.
about.a5CrewParagraph1: A dozen people across four countries, most of us remote from day one. We review each other's code like it is our own and we treat docs as a first-class feature.
about.a5CrewParagraph2: No tickets, no standups, no drama. Just a shared README, honest PRs, and a deep respect for the craft.
about.a7Heading: From a side project to a product people love
about.a7Paragraph: What started as a weekend experiment became the company we run today. We stayed small on purpose, kept the speed, and never stopped listening to the people using what we build.
about.a7Point1Body: We prototype before we commit. Most ideas die on a whiteboard — the ones that survive get real users within a week.
about.a7Point2Body: Deadlines are real, but shortcuts are not. We ship on time by cutting scope, never quality.
about.a7Point3Body: Every design review starts with user recordings. If it does not help a real person, it does not ship.
about.a7CtaHeading: Want to know what we are building next?
about.a7CtaBody: Join the newsletter or come say hi — we reply to everything.
about.a8Heading: Building the rails for the next wave of fintech
about.a8Subtext: We power payments for teams who refuse to settle for clunky banking software.
about.a8MissionBody: Make financial infrastructure boring again. When the plumbing just works, founders can spend their energy on product, not on compliance.
about.a8ApiBody: One API for payments, payouts, and balances. Idempotent by design, webhooks you can trust, and an SLA that keeps us awake at night.
about.a8FoundersBody: We met building payments at a large bank and left to do it right. Ten years later we are still here, still in the details.
about.a9Bio1: I am a developer who cares about the last 10% — the keyboard shortcuts, the empty states, the error messages that tell you what to do next.
about.a9Bio2: For eight years I have built web products for startups and enterprises alike. I write code that other people can read, and I would rather ship small than ship late.
about.a9WorkBody: I take full ownership: from the first mockup to the last deploy. TypeScript end to end, tests where they matter, and documentation you will actually want to read.
about.a12Heading: Great software is built by great people
about.a12Body: We are an independent studio of senior engineers and designers. No juniors on your project, no account managers between you and the work.
about.a12CultureBody: The culture that attracts people is also the culture that keeps them. We protect our rituals the way we protect our deadlines.
about.a12Card1Body: We sell working software, not slideware. Every proposal starts with a prototype.
about.a12Card2Body: Opinionated by design. We would rather tell you what we think than what you want to hear.
about.a12Card3Body: Weekly releases, daily check-ins, and a bias for shipping over debating.
about.a13Intro: Every company has a beginning. Ours is a story of stubbornness, luck, and a lot of late nights.
about.a13Chapter1Body: In 2016, three colleagues were laid off on the same Tuesday. By Friday we had a name, a website, and our first client: a bakery that needed a better ordering system.
about.a13Chapter2Body: The bakery grew, and so did we. One product became five, five became a platform, and a platform became the thing we now call our flagship. We almost lost it all twice — both times we learned something worth keeping.
about.a13Chapter2ImageAlt: The team in the early years
about.a13Chapter3Body: Forty people, twelve countries, one mission: software that respects the people who use it. We still answer our own support emails, and we still celebrate every single deploy.
about.a14Heading: We build products that outlive their hype
about.a14Body: Fifteen years in, we have seen every trend come and go. What stays is the work: thoughtful products, honest teams, and users who stick around.
about.a14GlobalBody: We hire for judgment, not for timezone. Our meetings are recorded, our docs are asynchronous, and our offices are wherever our people are.
about.a14Bullet1Body: Coverage from Sydney to San Francisco
about.a14Bullet3Body: Work from anywhere you do your best work
about.a15Heading: We turn bold ideas into products people keep using
about.a15Body: Strategy, design, and engineering under one roof. You bring the problem, we bring the experience — and the shipping discipline.
about.a15HelpBody: Whether you have a question or a full product roadmap, we would love to hear from you.
about.a16Heading: Everything you need, nothing you don't
about.a16Body: We are not the biggest agency in the room. We are the one that ships.
about.a16ExpertiseBody: Senior people on every project — average of 10 years of experience.
about.a16SupportBody: Real humans who reply within hours, not ticket queues that reply within weeks.
about.a16SecurityBody: SOC 2 aligned, encrypted at rest and in transit, and audited every year.
about.a16SpeedBody: First working demo in two weeks, not two quarters.
about.a16TransparencyBody: Open roadmaps, honest budgets, and a shared dashboard you can check anytime.
about.a16ScalabilityBody: Architecture that starts small and grows to millions of users without a rewrite.
about.a16CtaHeading: Ready to build something worth keeping?
about.a16CtaBody: Tell us what you are working on — we will tell you honestly if we are the right fit.
about.a17Tab1Body: We are a software company founded in 2015 with a simple belief: good software should feel inevitable. Our tools are used by teams in more than 40 countries, from two-person startups to Fortune 500s.
about.a17Tab2Body: Our mission is to remove the friction between an idea and its users. We build platforms that handle the hard infrastructure so your team can focus on the part only humans can do.
about.a17Tab3Body: In ten years we want software teams to spend their time on problems, not plumbing. Here is what we are working toward:
about.a17Tab3Bullet1Body: Deploy with a single command, everywhere.
about.a17Tab3Bullet2Body: Great products make their users smarter over time.
about.a17Tab3Bullet3Body: Public APIs, public status, public pricing.
about.a18Heading: We build for people who build
about.a18Body: A small, senior team obsessed with the developer experience — our own included. We eat our own dogfood, then make the recipe public.
about.a18Feature1Body: Decisions in days, deploys in minutes.
about.a18Feature2Body: Honest pricing, honest timelines, honest feedback.
about.a18MissionHeading: Make building software feel like a craft again
about.a18MissionBody: Somewhere between the dashboards and the compliance forms, we lost the joy of making. We are here to bring it back — one boring, reliable, beautiful tool at a time.
about.a18Principle1Body: Reliability is a feature. We document, test, and ship patches nobody celebrates — so nothing ever breaks at midnight.
about.a18Principle2Body: Every hire, every meeting, every feature must earn its place. We stay small so the quality stays high.
about.a18Principle3Body: Every codebase, every process, every community we touch should be slightly better when we leave.
about.a19Quote: We are not building the biggest company. We are building the best one we know how to build — one honest day of work at a time.
about.a19Body: Growth is easy to measure and hard to value. We optimize for the other numbers: how many users recommend us, how many people stay for years, how proud we are at the end of the week.
about.a28Heading: A place where work feels like craft
about.a28Body: Four walls, a lot of light, and the feeling that every detail was chosen on purpose.
about.a28ValueBody: We argue about typography with the same seriousness we argue about infrastructure. Because both end up in the product your users see.
about.a28Bullet1Body: Nothing ships without being seen by three pairs of eyes.
about.a28Bullet2Body: Every Friday afternoon is dedicated to experiments, talks, and side quests.
about.a28Bullet3Body: Docs updated, tests green, branch merged — no loose ends for the next person.

bento.bento4Tile1Summary: Trigger actions from any event in the workspace.

blogPost.blogPost1Heading: Design systems that scale with your team
blogPost.blogPost1Subheading: How a shared vocabulary of tokens and components keeps product teams moving fast without breaking the experience.
blogPost.blogPost1HeroAlt: Team sketching interface components on a whiteboard
blogPost.blogPost1Intro: Every product team eventually hits the same wall: interfaces drift, styles multiply, and shipping a new screen starts to feel like archaeology. A design system is the usual answer, but the hard part is never the tokens — it's keeping them alive after the launch post.
blogPost.blogPost1AlertBody: A design system only works if it reduces decisions. If your team spends more time debating the system than building with it, simplify the vocabulary first.
blogPost.blogPost1Section1Body: Design tokens are the single source of truth behind every color, space, and radius in the product. When a token changes, every screen updates with it. Components come second: they are recipes that combine tokens into repeatable patterns.
blogPost.blogPost1Section2Heading: Make the system the default path
blogPost.blogPost1Section2Body: The fastest way to kill a design system is to make it optional. New screens should start from existing components, and exceptions should be rare, named, and reviewed — otherwise the system decays into a museum.
blogPost.blogPost1Quote: A design system is not a deliverable. It is a decision-making tool the whole team lives in.
blogPost.blogPost1ListLead: Three habits that keep a system healthy:
blogPost.blogPost1List1: Review new patterns in the open, with product and engineering together.
blogPost.blogPost1List2: Measure adoption per release instead of celebrating launch-day hype.
blogPost.blogPost1List3: Retire unused tokens and components before they accumulate.
blogPost.blogPost1Closing: None of this is glamorous, and that is exactly the point. A system that quietly makes the right thing the easy thing is working. The moment it demands attention, it has stopped being a system and started being a project.
blogPost.blogPost2TabDescription: A longread with a sticky author card and share links.
blogPost.blogPost2AuthorBio: Maya writes about design systems, frontend architecture, and the slow craft of shipping well.
blogPost.blogPost2HeroAlt: Abstract architectural sketch of a component library
blogPost.blogPost2Lead: The best interfaces feel obvious in hindsight. Nobody claps when a button is exactly where they expected it — and that is the highest compliment a product can earn. This is the story of how one team got there, slowly and unglamorously.
blogPost.blogPost2Section1Body: For a year, the team shipped fast and paid for it later. Every screen introduced a new gray, a new spacing, a new way to show errors. The library grew, and so did the inconsistency. The turning point was not a redesign — it was admitting that style guides were documents, not systems.
blogPost.blogPost2Quote: Consistency is not sameness. It is the reliable repetition of a small set of decisions.
blogPost.blogPost2Section2Body: The team cut the token set in half, then in half again. Ten grays became three, four radii became two, and every component had to be built from that vocabulary or not exist at all. Constraints, it turned out, were the point.
blogPost.blogPost2List2: No new component without a written reason.
blogPost.blogPost2Section3Body: Adoption was not mandated; it was measured. Before long the fastest way to build a screen was also the most consistent one, and the numbers followed.
blogPost.blogPost2Closing: The moral is almost too obvious to write down: a system that makes the right thing easy will win without a single memo. The team stopped debating and started shipping — and the product got quieter, which is the best thing a product can do.

blogPost.blogPost3Heading: What shipped in our spring release
blogPost.blogPost3HeroAlt: Dashboard showing the new release notes
blogPost.blogPost3Section1Body: This release is about removing friction. We rebuilt the theming pipeline, introduced a new token hierarchy, and retired a decade of one-off overrides. The headline number: 41% fewer custom styles across the product.
blogPost.blogPost3AlertBody: Legacy theme files stop loading on May 1. Run the migration script before then — it converts most files automatically.
blogPost.blogPost3Section2Body: Tokens now live in one place and flow to every platform. Semantics are the only way to reference color, so dark mode no longer needs a parallel set of decisions.
blogPost.blogPost3Section3Body: Buttons, inputs, and cards were rebuilt on the new token map. Visually the change is subtle; structurally it is the largest refactor we have shipped since the first version.
blogPost.blogPost3Quote: The best release notes are the ones that make the old behavior feel obviously wrong.
blogPost.blogPost3Section4Body: Most code needs no changes. Custom color classes are the exception: replace them with semantic tokens and the surface theme handles the rest. Our tooling flags the rest on CI.
blogPost.blogPost3PromoBody: Join the beta list to try the new theming pipeline before the public launch.
blogPost.blogPost4TabDescription: A long article with breadcrumbs, a sticky share rail, and back to top.
blogPost.blogPost4Title: A practical guide to design tokens
blogPost.blogPost4Lead: Design tokens sound like infrastructure, which means most people ignore them until something breaks. This guide walks through what they actually are, how to name them without regret, and how to ship them without a rewrite. No theory — just the working parts.
blogPost.blogPost4Section1Body: A token is a named value — a color, a space, a radius — that stands for one decision in one place. When the value changes, every consumer updates. That single property is why teams adopt them and why abandoned systems feel so bad: the promise is real, but only while the pipeline is alive.
blogPost.blogPost4Section2Body: Name tokens by role, not appearance. 'primary' outlives 'blue-500' because roles survive redesigns. Layer primitives under semantics and keep the public surface small.
blogPost.blogPost4Section3Body: Ship tokens as code and as JSON, from the same source. Version them like any library: breaking changes behind a major bump, deprecations announced early, and a migration tool for the long tail.
blogPost.blogPost4AlertBody: Deprecation warnings only work if someone reads them. Surface them in the editor, not just in the changelog.
blogPost.blogPost4Quote: A token system is finished when adding a color feels more expensive than reusing one.
blogPost.blogPost4Section4Body: Every token needs an owner and a review path. The review is fast because the rule is simple: if it is not a role, it does not exist. New tokens are rare; changed tokens are rarer.
blogPost.blogPost5TabDescription: An editorial layout with a bold headline and an offset sidebar rail.
blogPost.blogPost5Heading: The quiet power of boring interfaces
blogPost.blogPost5HeroAlt: Minimal workspace with a single focused screen
blogPost.blogPost5HeroCaption: The best tools disappear into the work.
blogPost.blogPost5Section1Body: Nobody praises the airport for having clear signs — they just catch their flight. The same is true for software. When the interface is boring, the work becomes the center of attention, and that is when people do their best work.
blogPost.blogPost5Section2Body: Every pixel of decoration spends attention. A gradient, a shadow, a clever animation — each one is a withdrawal from the user's focus. The most productive interfaces are the ones that never ask for a deposit.
blogPost.blogPost5Quote: Design is not decoration. It is the removal of everything that gets in the way of intent.
blogPost.blogPost5AlertBody: Next time you build a screen, delete every style that does not carry meaning. Keep only what affects comprehension — you will be surprised what survives.
blogPost.blogPost5Section3Body: We compared a decorated checkout flow with a stripped-down one. The results were not subtle.
blogPost.blogPost5Section4Body: Boring is not lazy. It demands better typography, sharper copy, and ruthlessly consistent spacing — because nothing hides behind decoration. It is the harder craft, and it is worth it.
blogPost.blogPost6TabDescription: A long-form article with a dotted hero and a sticky chapter rail.
blogPost.blogPost6Heading: Designing for calm: a practical guide to quieter interfaces
blogPost.blogPost6Subtitle: How spacing, restraint and rhythm shape digital products that feel effortless to use.
blogPost.blogPost6Chapter1Paragraph1: Attention is the scarcest resource in any product. Every element we add competes for it, and most of them lose the moment they appear. Calm interfaces win by giving the eye fewer things to resolve and more room to breathe.
blogPost.blogPost6Chapter1Paragraph2: This is not minimalism for its own sake. It is the deliberate removal of noise so the content can carry the message alone.
blogPost.blogPost6Chapter2Paragraph1: Whitespace is not empty space; it is structural. A well-spaced layout tells the reader what belongs together and what deserves pause. Grouping, hierarchy and breathing room do more for comprehension than any border or shadow.
blogPost.blogPost6Chapter2Paragraph2: Start from the largest gaps and work inward. If spacing feels arbitrary, double it and reconsider — most layouts survive the test.
blogPost.blogPost6Chapter3Paragraph: A limited palette gives every accent meaning. When one color does the work of emphasis, users learn to trust it quickly. Reserve saturated hues for the moments that actually matter.
blogPost.blogPost6Chapter4Paragraph: Consistent rhythm makes reading feel effortless. Repeating patterns of space, type and motion let the mind anticipate what comes next, turning a long article into a pleasant walk instead of a scramble.
blogPost.blogPost6ConclusionParagraph: Quiet design is a discipline, not a style. It asks us to remove until only the essential remains — and then remove a little more. The result is software that feels considerate, and users who feel at ease.
blogPost.blogPost6AuthorBio: Maya designs interfaces for teams who value focus over friction. She writes about calm systems, typography and the craft of subtraction.
blogPost.blogPost6Figure1Alt: A minimal interface with generous whitespace
blogPost.blogPost6Figure2Alt: Spacing scale applied to a settings panel

blogPost.blogPost7Heading: The quiet power of tiny rituals
blogPost.blogPost7Description1: In a world built for urgency, the smallest recurring habits become anchors. A morning sketch, a midday walk, an evening page — each one a small act of orientation.
blogPost.blogPost7Description2: These rituals do not demand discipline. They reward presence. Over time they stack into something steadier than any plan: a life with texture, built one deliberate moment at a time.
blogPost.blogPost7ImageAlt: A writer's desk lit by soft morning light
blogPost.blogPost8TabDescription: A long-form article with a sticky numbered table of contents.
blogPost.blogPost8Summary: Release discipline is a quiet superpower. Here is how small teams ship reliable software by shrinking scope, staging risk and writing for the future reader.
blogPost.blogPost8Section1Paragraph1: Every feature spends from the same account: attention, testing, and future maintenance. Teams that treat scope like a budget ship faster because they are honest about what they can afford.
blogPost.blogPost8Section1Paragraph2: The best scope cut is the one that removes a decision, not just a screen. Fewer states mean fewer surprises, and fewer surprises mean calmer releases.
blogPost.blogPost8Section2Paragraph1: Big releases fail in public. Small ones fail in private. Splitting a launch into behind-the-flag steps lets a team watch real usage before committing to the roll out.
blogPost.blogPost8Section2Paragraph2: Shipping is a habit, and habits are built in small, repeatable motions. A team that ships weekly becomes good at shipping, and teams that are good at shipping become good at fixing.
blogPost.blogPost8Section3Paragraph: Code is read ten times more than it is written. Comments that explain why, names that state intent and pull requests that tell a story all reduce the cost of the next change.
blogPost.blogPost8Section4Paragraph: A release is not done when it ships; it is done when the team reflects. A short retrospective after each landing turns experience into a playbook instead of a memory.
blogPost.blogPost8Quote: The goal of a release is not to be perfect. It is to be observably better tomorrow than we are today.
blogPost.blogPost8HeroImageAlt: A calm engineering workspace at dusk
blogPost.blogPost9TabDescription: A single-column article with a share row and an author biography card.
blogPost.blogPost9Heading: Why we should read slowly again
blogPost.blogPost9Summary: Speed is the default setting of modern reading. Slowing down is not nostalgia; it is a way of reclaiming depth from the feed.
blogPost.blogPost9Section1Paragraph1: Skimming treats every text as a headline hunt. It optimizes coverage and sacrifices comprehension, leaving us informed about everything and changed by nothing.
blogPost.blogPost9Section1Paragraph2: Reading quickly is not the same as reading well. The best sentences are not transit stops; they are destinations.
blogPost.blogPost9Section2Paragraph1: Sustained attention is trained, not inherited. A page read without interruption is the literary equivalent of a long walk — and it strengthens the same quiet stamina.
blogPost.blogPost9Section2Paragraph2: Choose one text and read it to the end. The discomfort of staying with a single idea is the price of the depth it returns.
blogPost.blogPost9Section3Paragraph: Slow reading rewards patience unevenly. Some pages give back immediately; others wait years to matter. Trusting the process is part of the craft.
blogPost.blogPost9Quote: We do not read slowly because we have time. We read slowly because we refuse to spend attention faster than we earn it.
blogPost.blogPost9AuthorBio: Nora edits books by day and writes essays by night. Her work explores attention, memory and the quiet art of finishing things.
blogPost.blogPost9HeroImageAlt: An open book resting on a wooden table
blogPost.blogPost10TabDescription: A narrow reading column with a scroll-driven progress bar.
blogPost.blogPost10Heading: Notes on doing one thing at a time
blogPost.blogPost10Section1Paragraph1: We praise multitasking like a skill, yet every study quietly disagrees. What we call multitasking is usually task-switching, and every switch taxes attention with a small toll.
blogPost.blogPost10Section1Paragraph2: The fix is not discipline but design: decide once what matters, and let everything else wait its turn.
blogPost.blogPost10Section2Paragraph1: A single working block has three parts: a short planning step, a protected span of work, and a moment of honest review. The block does not need to be long to be real.
blogPost.blogPost10Section2Paragraph2: Protection matters more than duration. A thirty-minute span without interruption outperforms two distracted hours every time.
blogPost.blogPost10Section3Paragraph: Distraction announces itself softly. The discipline is not to avoid it, but to notice it early and return without self-punishment. Returning is the whole trick.
blogPost.blogPost10Section4Paragraph: Nothing builds momentum like a finished thing. Even a small completion changes how the next task feels; it converts obligation into choice.
blogPost.blogPost10Closing: The article ends here — which is exactly where the work begins.
blogPost.blogPost11TabDescription: Split hero with author row and a bordered pull-quote block
blogPost.blogPost11Heading: The quiet power of restraint in modern interface design
blogPost.blogPost11Lead: Great interfaces don't shout. They guide, pause, and let the content breathe — a closer look at why less still wins.
blogPost.blogPost11ImageAlt: Minimal workspace with a single chair beside a large window
blogPost.blogPost11Body1: Every element we remove is a decision we no longer have to defend. When a screen sheds its decorations, what remains is the task itself — and the user's attention finally has somewhere to land.
blogPost.blogPost11Quote: Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.
blogPost.blogPost11Body2: The most durable products treat visual hierarchy as a conversation. Headlines speak first, supporting text answers questions, and secondary actions stay politely out of the way until they are needed. This is not minimalism for its own sake; it is clarity as a competitive advantage.
blogPost.blogPost12TabDescription: Centered minimal essay with a floated serif drop cap
blogPost.blogPost12Title: Notes on reading slowly in a world built for speed
blogPost.blogPost12Paragraph1: Everything begins with attention, and attention begins with stillness. I used to skim articles the way people skim headlines on a crowded train — eyes moving faster than the words could settle. Then one evening I decided to read a single page of a novel aloud, and the world slowed down long enough for a thought to finish itself.
blogPost.blogPost12ImageAlt: Open book resting on a wooden table in soft morning light
blogPost.blogPost12Paragraph2: Speed is a habit, and like every habit it can be unlearned. A paragraph is not a file to be compressed; it is a room to be entered. When I stopped searching for conclusions and started sitting inside sentences, reading became less like consuming and more like listening.
blogPost.blogPost12Paragraph3: Every blank space on the page is a small promise: you may pause here. The generous margins of a well-set book are not wasted paper — they are the breathing room that turns printed words into a conversation with yourself.
blogPost.blogPost12Conclusion: Slow reading will not save the world, but it might save one hour of it — the one where a sentence finally means what it says.
blogPost.blogPost13TabDescription: Two-column article with sticky related links and newsletter
blogPost.blogPost13Title: Building a design system that survives contact with reality
blogPost.blogPost13Summary: Tokens are easy. Culture is hard. How one team kept its component library honest across fifteen product teams.
blogPost.blogPost13Paragraph1: Every design system begins with a beautiful grid of buttons and cards. It survives its first year because of what happens at the edges: the three-line address field, the error state nobody screenshotted, the legacy page that refuses to migrate.
blogPost.blogPost13Paragraph2: When the system accommodates these moments without shame, teams stop treating it as a constraint and start treating it as a tool. The difference is audible in standups: from "the system doesn't let me" to "how do we extend the system for this?"
blogPost.blogPost13Quote: A design system is a promise you keep every Tuesday, not a manifesto you publish once.
blogPost.blogPost13Paragraph3: The fastest way to kill adoption is a review board. Instead, we shipped token changes on Fridays, kept a public changelog, and let any team open a proposal. Approval became a conversation rather than a queue.
blogPost.blogPost13Paragraph4: Two years in, the system has no single owner and no single truth — and that is exactly why it keeps working. It belongs to everyone who ships with it.

caseStudy.caseStudy1Title: How Meridian Retail cut fulfillment time in half
caseStudy.caseStudy1Lead: A phased rollout of a new fulfillment engine took Meridian from overnight backlogs to same-day dispatch across 40 warehouses.
caseStudy.caseStudy1ChallengeBody: Order volume had tripled in two years, but Meridian's warehouse routing was still built for a fraction of that load. Pick times crept up, delivery promises slipped, and support tickets about late orders became the team's biggest time sink.
caseStudy.caseStudy1ApproachBody: We embedded with the fulfillment team for eight weeks, mapping every handoff from checkout to loading dock. A new routing engine prioritized orders by shipping deadline, and pickers got a redesigned mobile flow that cut walking distance per order by a third.
caseStudy.caseStudy1ResultBody: Same-day dispatch became the default rather than the exception. Within a year, Meridian was routing more than double the order volume through the same warehouse footprint, with room to keep scaling.
caseStudy.caseStudy1QuoteText: The new routing logic paid for itself in the first peak season. We finally stopped fighting the warehouse floor plan and started using it.
caseStudy.caseStudy1ReportDialogDescription: The highlights from Meridian's 12-month engagement, pulled straight from the final report.
caseStudy.caseStudy1ReportHighlight1: Same-day dispatch rate climbed from 61% to 97% across all 40 warehouses.
caseStudy.caseStudy1ReportHighlight2: Average picker walking distance dropped by 34% after the routing redesign.
caseStudy.caseStudy1ReportHighlight3: Support tickets tagged "late delivery" fell by more than half quarter over quarter.

caseStudy.caseStudy3OverviewHeading: A telehealth intake that lost patients before their first visit
caseStudy.caseStudy3OverviewBody: Solace Health's intake flow asked for insurance details, medical history and consent on a single long form. Nearly a third of new patients abandoned it before booking their first appointment, and clinics were left chasing missing information by phone.
caseStudy.caseStudy3StrategyHeading: Splitting intake into a guided sequence
caseStudy.caseStudy3StrategyBody: We broke the form into short, saveable steps that adapt to each patient's plan type, added inline verification for insurance IDs, and gave clinic staff a live view of where each patient dropped off.
caseStudy.caseStudy3ResultsHeading: Onboarding that finally keeps pace with demand
caseStudy.caseStudy3ResultsBody: Completion rates rose within the first month and kept climbing as the clinic team fine-tuned the follow-up prompts for stalled sessions.
caseStudy.caseStudy3TeamHeading: A small pod embedded with the clinic team
caseStudy.caseStudy3TeamBody: Four specialists worked directly alongside Solace Health's front-desk staff for the length of the engagement, sitting in on real intake calls to see the friction firsthand.

caseStudy.caseStudy8Title: Fernweg Travel rebuilds its booking engine on the fly
caseStudy.caseStudy8HeroAlt: Fernweg Travel booking interface on a laptop screen
caseStudy.caseStudy8Intro: Fernweg Travel needed to replace a decade-old booking engine without taking checkout offline for a single night of peak season. Here's how the migration shipped in the open, one route at a time.
caseStudy.caseStudy8Heading1: Shipping a new engine underneath a live product
caseStudy.caseStudy8Body1: Rather than a cutover weekend, the team ran the legacy and new booking engines side by side, routing a small slice of traffic to the new path each week and watching conversion and error rates before widening the rollout.
caseStudy.caseStudy8QuoteText: We never had a night where bookings just stopped. That was the entire point of going slow.
caseStudy.caseStudy8QuoteAttribution: Rasmus Iversen, Head of Engineering at Fernweg Travel
caseStudy.caseStudy8Body2: Beyond the migration itself, the new engine gave Fernweg's team a booking system fast enough to support real-time fare changes and multi-city itineraries that the old platform simply couldn't model.
caseStudy.caseStudy8CompanyTagline: Booking infrastructure for independent travel agencies
caseStudy.caseStudy8ScopeBody: A 14-week engagement covering system design, a phased traffic cutover and two weeks of post-launch monitoring support.

changelog.changelog5Entry1Body: Dashboards used to live inside a single saved view. Now you can combine any number of views, charts, and counters onto one canvas and pin it to your workspace sidebar so the whole team sees the same numbers on login.
changelog.changelog5Entry2Body: Setting up a new workspace from scratch was the single biggest complaint in our support queue. Templates capture folder structure, saved views, and permission defaults, so a new team is productive in minutes, not days.
changelog.changelog5Entry3Body: The old admin-or-member split didn't scale past a few dozen people. This release adds five built-in roles and per-folder visibility, with custom roles available on the Team plan for organizations with their own approval chains.
changelog.changelog5Entry4Body: We replaced the mobile app's data layer with an offline-first cache, which cut cold-start time by 70% and made switching between workspaces feel instant even on a slow connection.
changelog.changelog6TabDescription: A release card grid where icon actions and a full-detail dialog live on every entry.
changelog.changelog6Intro: Browse every release as a card, then open one for the full write-up.
changelog.changelog6Entry1Excerpt: Pin any combination of saved views to a shareable dashboard.
changelog.changelog6Entry1Body: Dashboards are no longer tied to a single saved view. Drag widgets onto a canvas, resize them, and pin the result to your workspace sidebar so the whole team opens the same numbers every morning.
changelog.changelog6Entry1Highlight1: Six widget types, including funnels and trend lines.
changelog.changelog6Entry1Highlight2: Dashboards load from cache instantly, then refresh in the background.
changelog.changelog6Entry2Excerpt: Turn a working workspace into a template new teams can start from.
changelog.changelog6Entry2Body: The template gallery captures folder structure, saved views, and default permissions from any workspace you designate. New teams pick a template and land in a working setup instead of a blank page.
changelog.changelog6Entry2Highlight1: Categorized templates for sales, support, and engineering.
changelog.changelog6Entry2Highlight2: Copying a template preserves filters and column layouts.
changelog.changelog6Entry3Excerpt: Five built-in roles with per-folder visibility replace admin/member.
changelog.changelog6Entry3Body: Fine-grained roles give every teammate exactly the access they need. Guests only see folders they've been explicitly invited to, and role changes now apply the moment you save them.
changelog.changelog6Entry3Highlight1: Custom roles available on the Team plan.
changelog.changelog6Entry3Highlight2: An audit log entry for every permission change.
changelog.changelog6Entry4Excerpt: An offline-first cache makes the mobile app dramatically faster.
changelog.changelog6Entry4Body: We rebuilt the mobile app's data layer around an offline-first cache. Cold starts are 70% faster, and switching workspaces on a slow connection now feels instant instead of stalling on a spinner.
changelog.changelog6Entry4Highlight1: Cold start down from 2.1s to 0.6s on average.
changelog.changelog6Entry4Highlight2: Offline edits sync automatically once you're back online.
changelog.changelog6Entry5Excerpt: A rebuilt core: faster search, a new sidebar, and a plugin API.
changelog.changelog6Entry5Body: Orbiter 2.0 is a ground-up rebuild of the core app. Search is now backed by a dedicated index, the sidebar has been redesigned around workspaces instead of folders, and a new plugin API lets you extend the app without waiting on us.
changelog.changelog6Entry5Highlight1: Search results now return in under 100ms.
changelog.changelog6Entry5Highlight2: Plugin API available in open beta.
changelog.changelog6Entry6Excerpt: A stable REST API and outbound webhooks for every workspace event.
changelog.changelog6Entry6Body: The public API graduates out of beta with a stable versioning policy, higher rate limits, and outbound webhooks for every workspace event — from item creation to permission changes.
changelog.changelog6Entry6Highlight1: Rate limits raised to 600 requests per minute.
changelog.changelog6Entry6Highlight2: Webhook payloads now include a verifiable signature header.
changelog.changelog8TabDescription: Long-form release write-ups next to an on-this-page sidebar that jumps and tracks scroll.
changelog.changelog8Intro: The reasoning behind the releases that mattered most, not just the bullet points.
changelog.changelog8Entry1Body: The most requested feature of the last year, by a wide margin. Dashboards can now pull from any saved view across the workspace, not just one at a time, and the whole thing renders from cache before quietly refreshing in the background — so it never feels like a loading screen.
changelog.changelog8Entry2Body: Onboarding a new team used to mean copying folders by hand or starting from nothing. Templates snapshot a workspace's structure, views, and default permissions, so the next team starts from something that already works.
changelog.changelog8Entry3Body: This one took two quarters longer than planned, mostly because we rewrote the permission checks three times to keep them fast at scale. Five built-in roles now cover most teams, with custom roles for the organizations that need their own approval chains.
changelog.changelog8Entry4Body: Cold starts on mobile had crept up to over two seconds. An offline-first cache brought that down to under a second and made switching between workspaces feel instant, even on airplane wifi.
changelog.changelog8Entry5Body: Everything after this entry was built on a foundation we laid here: a dedicated search index, a workspace-first sidebar, and a plugin API we're still building on top of ourselves.

compare.compare2Sub1Body: Forge suits solo makers and small teams that need a dependable editor on a modest budget. Its plan limits become noticeable once you add more than a handful of collaborators, which is why most growing teams move to Nimbus within the first year.
compare.compare2Sub2Body: The core editor experience is close, but the two products diverge sharply on collaboration, automation, and support. Forge treats premium features as add-ons, while Nimbus includes real-time collaboration, full metadata history, and priority support in every plan.

content.content1TabDescription: Long-form article with a hero image and a sticky outline rail that highlights the section in view.
content.content1Subtext: A few durable habits that keep a product feeling calm long after the launch confetti settles.
content.content1HeroAlt: Wide editorial photograph accompanying the article
content.content1Section1Paragraph: Every interface begins with too many ideas and not enough discipline. The fastest way to make a screen feel considered is to remove the element you were proudest of and see if anyone notices it's gone. If nobody does, it wasn't load-bearing — it was decoration wearing a badge that said 'feature.'
content.content1Section2Paragraph: Long before a user reads a single word, the type is already telling them how the product feels about itself — confident, cautious, playful, exhausted. A consistent type scale does more for perceived quality than another round of color tweaks, because it's the one decision a reader can't help but notice on every single screen.
content.content1Section3Heading: Motion is a seasoning, not a meal
content.content1Section3Paragraph: Animation should explain a change, not perform one. The best transitions are the ones a user can't describe afterward, because they only remember what happened, not how it moved. If a reviewer's first note is 'love the animation,' the animation was standing in for something the interface should have said on its own.
content.content1Section4Paragraph: The empty state, the error, the slow network, and the second time a user opens the same screen — these are the four moments that decide whether a product feels trustworthy. Sketch those before the happy path, because the happy path is the one moment nobody remembers being careful about.
content.content2TabDescription: Content hub explainer with filter chips and a grid of content-type cards.
content.content2Heading: Everything we publish, organized by how you like to learn
content.content2Subtext: Filter by format to jump straight to guides, tutorials, videos, or conversations with the team.
content.content2Type1Desc: Short, opinionated walkthroughs for the first hour with a new tool.
content.content2Type2Desc: The exhaustive version — every setting, every edge case, kept current.
content.content2Type3Desc: Build something real, step by step, with the finished project at the end.
content.content2Type4Desc: Line-by-line explanations of the trickier parts of the codebase.
content.content2Type5Desc: Recorded sessions and short screencasts for when reading isn't enough.
content.content2Type6Desc: Conversations with the people who built the thing about why they built it that way.
content.content3TabDescription: Deep guide with breadcrumbs, a vertical chapter rail, and a reading-progress bar.
content.content3Subtext: Everything you need to take a project from a single laptop to a server you actually trust, in four chapters.
content.content3Chapter1Paragraph: Before touching a terminal, it helps to know what you're building toward: one process that serves requests, one process that stores data, and a boundary between them that you control. Everything else in this guide is detail in service of that one sentence.
content.content3Chapter1Takeaway: You need exactly two long-running processes to start — everything else can wait until it's actually slowing you down.
content.content3Chapter2Heading: What to have ready before you start
content.content3Chapter2Paragraph: You'll want a machine with at least two cores and four gigabytes of memory, a domain you can point somewhere, and about twenty uninterrupted minutes. None of the steps that follow are hard on their own — they're just easy to get out of order.
content.content3Chapter2Takeaway: Write down your domain and server IP before you start; half of setup trouble is copy-pasting the wrong one.
content.content3Chapter3Paragraph: Configuration is where most guides lose people, mainly because they explain every option instead of the three that matter: where data lives, which port answers requests, and which secret signs your sessions. Get those three right and the rest is convenience.
content.content3Chapter3Takeaway: Generate a fresh session secret for every environment — never copy one over from a tutorial or a previous project.
content.content3Chapter4Paragraph: Almost every first-run failure traces back to one of two causes: a port already in use, or a configuration value the process expected but never received. Check both before you suspect anything more exotic — exotic bugs are rarer than tired eyes skimming a log.
content.content3Chapter4Takeaway: Read the first error in the log, not the last — everything after it is usually just the fallout.
content.content4TabDescription: Long article with an author byline row and a pill-style section switcher.
content.content4Subtext: A calmer release process isn't slower — it just moves the panic to a place where nobody can see it.
content.content4OutlineAria: Jump to a section of this article
content.content4Section1Paragraph: Teams that ship calmly aren't lucky, and they aren't slower than everyone else — they've just moved the stressful part earlier, into a rehearsal nobody watches, instead of leaving it for the release nobody can undo. The adrenaline has to go somewhere; the only question is whether you choose where.
content.content4Section2Paragraph: Every release ships through the exact same path a rollback would take, so the emergency exit is never a surprise on the one day you need it. We rehearse the boring version of launch day so often that the real one stops feeling like an event.
content.content4Section2Quote: The safest release is the one that looks exactly like the last nine you didn't think twice about.
content.content4Section2FigureAlt: Photograph illustrating the calm, rehearsed rhythm of a release day
content.content4Section3Paragraph: None of this is free. Rehearsal takes time you could spend building, and a boring process is a hard sell to anyone who equates urgency with progress. We've made peace with shipping slightly less often in exchange for never once needing a 2 a.m. apology to customers.
content.content4Section4Paragraph: The next habit we're building is treating the rollback itself as a feature worth testing on purpose, not just a plan we hope to never open. A recovery path nobody has rehearsed is really just a theory.
content.content4FeedbackThanks: Thanks — that helps us write the next one.

helpCenter.helpCenter2Q1: How do I reset my password?
helpCenter.helpCenter2A1: Open Settings, then Security, and choose Reset password. We'll email you a secure link that expires in 30 minutes.
helpCenter.helpCenter2Q2: Can I change my subscription plan?
helpCenter.helpCenter2A2: Yes. Upgrades apply immediately and downgrades take effect at the end of your current billing cycle.
helpCenter.helpCenter2A3: Go to Members, then Invite, and enter their email addresses. Invited teammates get access as soon as they accept.
helpCenter.helpCenter2Q4: Where can I find my API key?
helpCenter.helpCenter2A4: API keys live under Developer settings. Generate a new key at any time; existing keys keep working until you revoke them.
helpCenter.helpCenter2A5: We take encrypted snapshots every six hours and retain the last 30 days, so recovery is always available on request.
helpCenter.helpCenter2Q6: How do I cancel my account?
helpCenter.helpCenter2A6: Cancel anytime from Settings, then Billing. Your data stays available for 30 days in case you change your mind.

ourStory.ourStory1Heading: From a Weekend Prototype to a Company
ourStory.ourStory1Intro: Four eras, one obsession: making the tools we wished we had.
ourStory.ourStory1Era1Body: We built the first version in a rented co-working room, shipping fixes between day jobs until the side project outgrew the nights and weekends.
ourStory.ourStory1Era1ImageAlt: Two founders working on laptops at a small desk in an early co-working space
ourStory.ourStory1Era1Milestone1: First line of code written in a borrowed office
ourStory.ourStory1Era1Milestone2: Left our day jobs to work on it full-time
ourStory.ourStory1Era2Body: Word of mouth brought in customers faster than we could support them, so we hired our first engineers and put a proper roadmap on the wall.
ourStory.ourStory1Era2ImageAlt: Small team gathered around a whiteboard planning a product roadmap
ourStory.ourStory1Era3Body: A second office and a fully remote engineering team let us support customers around the clock, in more languages than we ever expected to need.
ourStory.ourStory1Era3ImageAlt: Team members video calling colleagues from a bright open-plan office
ourStory.ourStory1Era3Milestone2: Shipped support for a dozen languages
ourStory.ourStory1Era4Body: The team has grown, but the questions haven't changed: what's slow, what's confusing, and what can we make disappear for the people who use this every day.
ourStory.ourStory1Era4ImageAlt: Current team standing together at the company's present-day headquarters
ourStory.ourStory1Era4Milestone2: Still shipping something new every week
ourStory.ourStory1TabDescription: Company history split into tabbed eras, each pairing a milestone photo with founding highlights.
ourStory.ourStory2Intro: Five milestones, replayed automatically — pause anytime to read at your own pace.
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone1Body: A frustrating afternoon spent fighting spreadsheets convinced us there had to be a better way, and we started sketching one on a napkin that night.
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone1ImageAlt: Hand-drawn product sketch on a napkin next to a coffee cup
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone2Body: A small logistics team took a chance on our beta and never left, teaching us more about the problem than any amount of research could have.
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone2ImageAlt: Handshake between two people closing a first customer deal
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone3Body: We brought on our first designer and support lead, finally freeing up time to think past the next bug fix.
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone3ImageAlt: New team members introducing themselves around a conference table
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone4Body: Traffic tripled in a single quarter, and the infrastructure we'd patched together finally got the rebuild it deserved.
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone4ImageAlt: Engineers monitoring dashboards during a high-traffic scaling event
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone5Body: The napkin sketch is long gone, but the instinct behind it — build the tool you wish existed — still runs the roadmap.
ourStory.ourStory2Milestone5ImageAlt: Current product team reviewing the roadmap in a modern office
ourStory.ourStory2TabDescription: Auto-advancing milestone showcase with a segmented progress bar and pause control.
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter1Body: Why did the tools we used every day feel like they were working against us instead of for us?
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter1ImageAlt: Founder staring thoughtfully at a laptop screen late at night
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter2Body: No investors, no roadmap — just a small team convinced the answer was worth chasing.
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter2ImageAlt: Small team building an early prototype at a cluttered desk
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter3Body: A handful of early users became a hundred, then a thousand, each one shaping what we built next.
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter3ImageAlt: Crowd of early adopters gathered at a product launch event
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter4Body: That's when the company most people know today actually started — everything before it was just the rehearsal.
ourStory.ourStory3Chapter4ImageAlt: Full team celebrating together in the current headquarters
ourStory.ourStory3TabDescription: Full-bleed photo hero that reveals the founding story one chapter at a time.
ourStory.ourStory4SidebarBody: A quick look at the milestones that took Acme from a two-person team to the platform thousands of companies rely on every day.
ourStory.ourStory4Entry1Body: Two co-founders leave their jobs to build the product they couldn't find anywhere else.
ourStory.ourStory4Entry2Body: After eight months of nights and weekends, the first paying customers get access to the beta.
ourStory.ourStory4Entry3Body: The team outgrows the kitchen table and moves into a proper office with room to grow.
ourStory.ourStory4Entry4Body: New funding lets the team double in size and invest in the infrastructure customers were asking for.
ourStory.ourStory4Entry5Body: The product crosses a milestone nobody expected to hit this fast: one million registered accounts.
ourStory.ourStory4Entry6Body: Acme now supports teams in dozens of countries, with the same small-team focus it started with.
ourStory.ourStory4TabDescription: Sticky company profile beside a vertical timeline of key dates.
ourStory.ourStory5Intro: Hover or select a year to see how the idea grew, one decision at a time.
ourStory.ourStory5Year1Body: The very first version of the idea was a rough diagram drawn during a slow Tuesday lunch.
ourStory.ourStory5Year1ImageAlt: Napkin sketch of an early product idea on a cafe table
ourStory.ourStory5Year2Body: We traded the kitchen table for a shared desk in a co-working space and started taking the idea seriously.
ourStory.ourStory5Year2ImageAlt: Shared co-working desk with two laptops and notebooks
ourStory.ourStory5Year3Body: The first hires joined, bringing skills neither of us had and opinions we badly needed.
ourStory.ourStory5Year3ImageAlt: New teammates meeting for the first time around a small office table
ourStory.ourStory5Year4Body: The office emptied out overnight, and we rebuilt how the team worked from the ground up.
ourStory.ourStory5Year4ImageAlt: Team member working from a home office during a video call
ourStory.ourStory5Year5Body: A custom-built space finally gave the team room to design, build, and test in one place again.
ourStory.ourStory5Year5ImageAlt: Modern design studio space with the current team at work
ourStory.ourStory5TabDescription: Year-by-year story list that swaps the photo and copy on hover or selection.
ourStory.ourStory6Heading: A Hundred Years in the Making
ourStory.ourStory6Intro: Scroll through six chapters of the workshop that became a company.
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter1Body: A small workshop opens above a hardware store, building furniture to order for the neighborhood.
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter1ImageAlt: Black and white photo of an early twentieth-century furniture workshop
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter2Body: Three generations in, the family finally opens a storefront of its own on the high street.
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter2ImageAlt: Vintage storefront with large display windows on a busy street
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter3Body: A simple catalog website lets customers browse from home for the first time, and orders double within a year.
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter3ImageAlt: Late 1990s desktop computer displaying an early e-commerce catalog page
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter4Body: What was once a family business hires its first employees from outside the family to keep up with demand.
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter4ImageAlt: Growing team gathered in a busy workshop and office space
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter5Body: A fire damages the original workshop, and the team rebuilds it from the ground up with modern tools.
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter5ImageAlt: Newly rebuilt workshop with modern equipment and natural light
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter6Body: The workshop still stands on the same street, run by people who grew up hearing these stories firsthand.
ourStory.ourStory6Chapter6ImageAlt: Current team standing in front of the century-old workshop today
ourStory.ourStory6TabDescription: Horizontally scrolling chapter cards tracing a century of company history.

project.project1TabDescription: A full-width hero image leads into a two-column brief — project narrative on the left, a sticky client and stack card with a credits dialog on the right.
project.project1Summary: A ground-up redesign of Northbridge Bank's mobile app, focused on making transfers, budgeting, and card controls feel instant instead of buried three menus deep.
project.project1HeroAlt: Screens from the redesigned Northbridge mobile banking app shown side by side
project.project1OverviewBody: Northbridge's app had grown one feature at a time for six years, and it showed. Support tickets kept citing the same three tasks — moving money, checking a budget, freezing a card — as the hardest to find. We rebuilt the core flows around those three jobs first.
project.project1ApproachBody: We ran weekly usability sessions with existing customers throughout, testing paper flows before a single screen was built in code. Each round fed straight back into the next week's design, so the interface earned its shape rather than assumed it.
project.project1CreditsDialogDescription: The team behind the Northbridge redesign.
project.project2TabDescription: An edge-to-edge image carousel with a floating glass panel overlaying the current slide, showing the project title and a live slide counter.
project.project2Title: Alder & Pine — a boutique hotel identity
project.project2Tagline: Brand identity, signage, and a booking-first website for a 12-room hotel on the Oregon coast.
project.project2Description: Alder & Pine needed a brand that felt as unhurried as the stay itself — warm paper stock, a quiet color palette, and a website where booking a room takes under a minute on a phone with one bar of signal.
project.project2Slide1Alt: The Alder & Pine hotel entrance with new signage
project.project2Slide2Alt: A guest room styled with the new Alder & Pine textile palette
project.project2Slide3Alt: The Alder & Pine booking website open on a laptop
project.project2Slide4Alt: Printed stationery and room keys carrying the new Alder & Pine mark
project.project3TabDescription: A structured brief pairs a problem-and-solution narrative with a formal specs table, deliverables checklist, and stack chips.
project.project3Intro: A ten-year-old dispatch tool was rebuilt from the ground up so dispatchers could see a driver's status, route, and delay risk without switching between four separate screens.
project.project3ProblemBody: Dispatchers were running three browser tabs and a printed route sheet just to answer 'where is this truck.' Shift handoffs lost context constantly, and delay alerts arrived only after a customer had already called to complain.
project.project3SolutionBody: One dashboard now surfaces live position, route progress, and a delay-risk score per driver, with handoff notes attached to the shift instead of a sticky note. Dispatchers open one screen at the start of a shift and rarely leave it.
project.project4TabDescription: A four-part project story scrolls past a sticky sidebar that tracks which phase is currently in view.
project.project4Title: Moving Loomcraft Goods off a legacy cart
project.project4Subtitle: A phased migration off a decade-old e-commerce platform, told in four stages: discovery, design, build, and launch.
project.project4Section1Heading: Finding out what was actually breaking checkout
project.project4Section1Body: Session recordings showed shoppers abandoning at shipping calculation nearly a third of the time. The old platform quoted shipping only after account creation, so we started there instead of guessing at a full redesign.
project.project4Section2Heading: Designing a checkout that shows its work early
project.project4Section2Body: Shipping and tax now estimate from the cart page, before any account is required. We tested three checkout lengths with real shoppers and shipped the shortest one that didn't hurt address accuracy.
project.project4Section3Heading: Building the migration without a launch-day cutover
project.project4Section3Body: Both platforms ran side by side for six weeks behind a traffic-split flag, so we could roll back a broken checkout variant in minutes instead of reverting a full deploy.
project.project4Section4Heading: Launching to 100% and retiring the old cart
project.project4Section4Body: Once the new checkout held steady at full traffic for two weeks, we decommissioned the legacy platform. Cart abandonment at the shipping step dropped by more than half.
project.project5TabDescription: A single centered column keeps the brief short — a quick-facts strip, one image, and a closing call to action.
project.project5Title: A portfolio built around negative space
project.project5Summary: Iris Vance needed a portfolio that got out of the way of the photographs — no filters, no carousels, just large prints and enough white space to breathe.
project.project5HeroAlt: A large-format print from the Iris Vance portfolio site
project.project5Body: Show one photograph at a time, full width, and get the interface out of the way — no navigation chrome longer than the alt text underneath it.
project.project6TabDescription: A draggable slider reveals the after state over the before screenshot, framed by outcome stats and the stack used to get there.
project.project6Title: Vantage CRM: from spreadsheet-in-a-browser to something usable
project.project6Summary: A visual and structural overhaul of an internal CRM that had accumulated a decade of one-off features with no shared layout language.
project.project6BeforeAlt: The original Vantage CRM interface, dense with unlabeled columns
project.project6AfterAlt: The redesigned Vantage CRM interface with a clear record layout
project.project6SliderCaption: Drag to compare the original screen against the redesign
project.project6StoryBody: Every screen shared the same twelve-column table with no visual hierarchy, so we rebuilt the record view around the three fields a rep actually needs in the first five seconds — and moved everything else behind one click.

resource.resource1Title: The State of Async-First Engineering Teams
resource.resource1Lead: We surveyed 400 engineering leads to find out how async-first teams ship faster without more meetings. Here's what separates the top performers.
resource.resource1Body1: Distributed teams no longer treat overlap hours as a given. The best-performing teams in our survey default to written proposals and recorded walkthroughs, reserving live time for the handful of decisions that truly need a room.
resource.resource1QuoteText: We cut our weekly meeting load in half and shipped more in the following quarter than in the two before it combined.
resource.resource1QuoteAttribution: VP of Engineering, mid-market SaaS company
resource.resource1Heading2: What the top quartile does differently
resource.resource1Body2: High-performing teams write decisions down before they're final, not after. That single habit accounts for most of the gap between the top and bottom quartile in our data.
resource.resource1Takeaway1: Async-first teams ship 30% more releases per quarter on average
resource.resource1Takeaway2: Written proposals cut decision time nearly in half
resource.resource1Takeaway3: Fewer than 20% of top performers hold daily standups

timeline.timeline1TabDescription: A centered vertical timeline with milestone cards alternating left and right along a connecting line.
timeline.timeline2TabDescription: A horizontally scrollable strip of launch-phase cards linked by a connecting line, with prev/next controls.

timeline.timeline4TabDescription: A conference-style agenda where each entry expands on click to reveal the speaker and location.
timeline.timeline5TabDescription: A filterable product roadmap with done, in-progress, and planned status badges plus an overall progress bar.
timeline.timeline6TabDescription: A bare-bones two-column list pairing dates with short history entries, with no cards or icons.
timeline.timeline7TabDescription: An interactive step indicator for exploring an order's progress from placement through delivery.
timeline.timeline8TabDescription: A vertical numbered walkthrough connecting icon badges for a simple sign-up-to-launch process.
timeline.timeline1Intro: A handful of moments that shaped where the company stands today, from a two-person prototype to a team working across a dozen countries.
timeline.timeline1Milestone1Description: Two founders and a shared desk — the first prototype went out to a handful of friendly testers within three months.
timeline.timeline1Milestone2Description: Word of mouth carried the product past its first real revenue milestone, long before any paid marketing existed.
timeline.timeline1Milestone3Description: The team outgrew the kitchen table and moved into a proper office, growing to forty people within the year.
timeline.timeline1Milestone4Description: Localization, regional pricing, and a distributed support team turned a single-market product into a global one.
timeline.timeline1Milestone5Description: Recognition from the industry for a decision made back in 2019: build something people actually want to use daily.
timeline.timeline2Intro: Five phases carry the product from a private alpha to a full enterprise rollout. Scroll sideways to walk through each one.
timeline.timeline2Phase1Description: A closed group of twenty teams gets early access to stress-test the core workflow and file rough-edge reports.
timeline.timeline2Phase2Description: Access opens to the waitlist. Onboarding gets rewritten twice based on what the alpha group struggled with.
timeline.timeline2Phase3Description: Anyone can sign up. Usage-based limits stay in place while the infrastructure is load-tested at scale.
timeline.timeline2Phase4Description: The beta tag comes off, billing goes live, and the product ships with a public changelog and status page.
timeline.timeline2Phase5Description: SSO, audit logs, and a dedicated onboarding track open the door to larger organizations.
timeline.timeline3Intro: A running log of features, improvements, and fixes, newest first. Tags call out what kind of change each entry is.
timeline.timeline3Entry1Description: A full dark theme across every dashboard screen, including charts and data tables, with a system-preference default.
timeline.timeline3Entry2Description: New records now show up in search results within seconds instead of the previous multi-minute delay.
timeline.timeline3Entry3Title: Fixed export timeout on large reports
timeline.timeline3Entry3Description: Reports over 50,000 rows no longer time out mid-export; large exports now stream to a downloadable file instead.
timeline.timeline3Entry4Description: Admins can now assign granular roles per workspace instead of the previous all-or-nothing member access.
timeline.timeline3Entry5Description: A race condition in the notification queue occasionally sent the same email twice; that path is now deduplicated.
timeline.timeline3Entry6Description: New accounts now reach their first working project in three steps instead of the previous seven-screen setup.
timeline.timeline4Intro: Four sessions run through the day. Expand a session to see who's speaking and where to find the room.
timeline.timeline4Event1Description: A look back at the year's biggest releases and a preview of what the roadmap has planned for the next twelve months.
timeline.timeline4Event2Description: How the design system evolved to support ten times the components without losing visual consistency.
timeline.timeline4Event3Description: A hands-on session covering authentication, pagination, and webhooks — bring a laptop and follow along.
timeline.timeline4Event4Description: Open questions from the audience, answered live by a panel of engineers, designers, and support leads.
timeline.timeline5Intro: A running view of what's shipped, what's underway, and what's still on the drawing board. Filter by status to focus on one stage.
timeline.timeline5Item1Description: Upload a CSV of up to 50,000 rows and map columns to fields without writing a single line of code.
timeline.timeline5Item2Description: Optional TOTP-based two-factor login, enforceable per workspace by an admin.
timeline.timeline5Item3Description: Drag-and-drop widgets to build a dashboard that matches how each team actually works.
timeline.timeline5Item4Description: A ground-up redesign of the mobile app around the three flows people use most on the go.
timeline.timeline5Item5Description: A cleaner, versioned API with cursor-based pagination and first-class webhook support.
timeline.timeline5Item6Description: Ask a question in plain language and get a chart pulled straight from your own workspace data.
timeline.timeline6Intro: A short, plain record of the moments worth remembering, in the order they happened.
timeline.timeline6Entry1Text: Registered the company name and reserved the domain.
timeline.timeline6Entry2Text: Shipped the first internal prototype to five pilot users.
timeline.timeline6Entry3Text: Closed a pre-seed round to fund the first two hires.
timeline.timeline6Entry5Text: Opened a second office to support growing regional demand.
timeline.timeline6Entry6Text: Passed an independent security audit with no critical findings.
timeline.timeline6Entry7Text: Reached 500,000 active users across forty countries.
timeline.timeline7Intro: Click any step to preview what happens at that stage, from the moment an order is placed to the moment it arrives.
timeline.timeline7Step1Description: We've received the order and it's queued for processing at the nearest warehouse.
timeline.timeline7Step2Description: The items are being picked, checked, and packed for handoff to the courier.
timeline.timeline7Step3Description: The package has left the warehouse and is now in transit toward the delivery address.
timeline.timeline7Step4Description: A courier has the package on their route today, with delivery expected by the end of the day.
timeline.timeline7Step5Description: The package was delivered and signed for. A confirmation email went out with the delivery photo.
timeline.timeline8Intro: Four short steps stand between a new account and a fully configured workspace — most teams finish in under ten minutes.
timeline.timeline8Step1Description: Sign up with an email address or continue with a social provider — no credit card required to start.
timeline.timeline8Step2Description: Click the confirmation link we send you to unlock the workspace and secure the account.
timeline.timeline8Step3Description: Set a workspace name, invite teammates, and turn on the integrations the team actually needs.
timeline.timeline8Step4Description: The workspace is ready. Start building right away, and invite the rest of the team whenever you're set.
